youtube.title: Listen to the cup fill | Reality Rulebook Season 2 · Episode 5
youtube.caption:
Can you hear a cup fill? Eyes closed, just listening.

The empty space above the water acts like a pipe closed at the water end. Sound bounces up and down inside it, and a short pipe rings higher than a long one. So as the water rises, the pitch climbs. In our simple model, ten centimeters of air rings near 690 vibrations a second and two centimeters near 1,900.

Season 2 · Episode 5.

Sources
1. Bagad, Tapaswi, Snoek, Zisserman, 'The Sound of Water: Inferring Physical Properties from Pouring Liquids', arXiv:2411.11222 (ICASSP 2025) (text read by the builder, not yet by a person): https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.11222
2. OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 17.5 Sources of Musical Sound (text read by the builder, not yet by a person): https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/17-5-sources-of-musical-sound
3. Our own computation from the paper's formula (compile.py): f = c / (4 (l + 0.62 R)), c = 343 m/s, R = 4 cm; the paper is Bagad et al., arXiv:2411.11222 (read in full by the builder) (compile.py, scene.mjs; made-up cup; model-check): https://github.com/arzateruben22/Claude/tree/claude/physics-s2/films/channels/physics/ep11

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Animation: code-rendered, no stock footage. The cup, the pipe and the numbers are our own simple model (an illustrated cup with made-up size); the pouring is an illustration, not a recording. The sources were read by the builder, not yet opened by a person.

Reality Rulebook: Everyday things, slowed down until the physics shows.
